sections.heading: Why the two small benchmarks are saturated
Ten ways a published score misleads
How to read a memory claim

slides.title: What the benchmarks *measure*
slides.text: Two schools of scoring, six benchmarks, ten ways a score misleads.

narration: A memory benchmark gives a system a long conversation.
Then it asks questions about it.
There are two ways to score the result.
One checks whether the right passage was found.
The other checks whether the final answer was right.
They are different questions with different numbers.
Most published claims quote one while the reader assumes the other.

slides.caption: A memory benchmark asks questions about a long conversation. There are two ways to score it, and most claims quote one while the reader assumes the other.

slides.title: What we will *cover*

narration: First, the two schools of scoring, and why they never share a table.
Then the six benchmarks that matter in September 2026.
Then why the two best-known benchmarks are saturated.
Then the dispute between the two largest vendors, as documented in public.
Then ten documented ways a published score misleads.
Last, five questions to ask before believing any number.

slides.caption: The two schools of scoring and the six benchmarks that matter. Why two are saturated and the vendor dispute of 2025. Ten ways a score misleads and five questions to ask.

slides.title: The retrieval school: was it *found*
slides.text: What fraction of the evidence reached the top k?

narration: The retrieval school measures recall at k.
Of the units marked as evidence, what fraction sits in the top k the system returns.
The standard form is the TREC fraction, computed by shared tools.
A looser variant is called any-hit.
It scores a full hit when at least one gold unit is in the top k.
It is always higher when a question has more than one piece of evidence.
The retrieval school is honest about what it leaves out.
No answer is generated.
So nothing is known about whether a reader could use what was found.

slides.caption: Retrieval recall at k asks what fraction of the gold evidence sits in the top k results. No answer is generated. The standard form is the TREC fraction.

slides.title: The answer school: was it *right*
slides.text: Did the answer come out right, by whose judge?

narration: The answer school runs a reader over what was retrieved.
Then it scores the answer.
By word overlap against a reference, or by a model acting as judge.
This is what the two best-known benchmark papers score.
It depends on the reader and on the judge.
There is no standard judge prompt.
So two systems scored by two vendors are not on the same scale, even on the same benchmark.

slides.caption: A reader answers from what was retrieved. The answer is scored by word overlap or by a model as judge. It depends on the reader and the judge.

slides.title: Two schools, *two tables*
slides.text: A retrieval score and an answer score never share a table.

narration: Both schools of scoring are legitimate, and neither is the lesser.
The only error is to place a retrieval number beside an answer number and read them as one thing.
A retrieval score is always higher than the answer score on the same system.
Every table in this section says which school it belongs to.
And no table holds both.

slides.caption: Both schools are legitimate. The only error is to place a retrieval-only number beside an answer number and read them as one thing.

slides.title: The six benchmarks that *matter*
head: Benchmark
Corpus per question
State

narration: Six benchmarks matter in September 2026.
The first has ten conversations of 16 to 26 thousand tokens and nearly two thousand questions.
Vendors report 92 to 95 on it.
The second has 500 questions over about 115 thousand tokens each, with a fixed judge.
Vendors report 90 to 94.
The third reaches ten million tokens, with two thousand questions across ten abilities.
The best published score there is 0.36 at half a million tokens and 0.27 at ten million.
The fourth tests retrieval, learning, long-range reading and forgetting.
The best system scores under 50, and every method fails multi-hop forgetting.
The fifth finds that full context scores 70 to 82 even on its hardest cases.
Its authors say retrieval is unnecessary below about 150 conversations.
The sixth passes ten million tokens, to 115 million tokens of agent trajectories.
A file-storing agent scores 72.5 there, against 48.5 for retrieval.

slides.caption: LoCoMo and LongMemEval are saturated. BEAM and MemoryAgentBench are far from it. ConvoMem finds retrieval unnecessary below 150 conversations. LongMemEval-V2 passes ten million tokens.

slides.title: Five more in 2026 say the *same*
slides.text: No architecture wins everywhere, and plain retrieval keeps up.

narration: Five more benchmarks appeared between February and August 2026.
Each reports the same two things in its own words.
Plain retrieval or plain long context stays competitive with dedicated memory systems.
And strong scores on factual recall do not carry over to using the memory well.
One June 2026 study ran twelve systems on eleven datasets.
It found no architecture that wins everywhere.

slides.caption: Five benchmarks from February to August 2026 report the same two things. Plain retrieval or plain long context stays competitive. Factual scores do not carry over to using the memory.

slides.title: Why the first benchmark is *saturated*
items: Category labels differ from the paper

narration: The first benchmark's conversations run 16 to 26 thousand tokens.
Every frontier model reads that in one call.
The largest vendor's own paper reports full context at 72.90, above its best memory variant at 68.44.
The released data has known defects.
The scorer's code treats category one as multi-hop.
The paper lists single-hop first.
So vendor tables disagree with each other on which category is which.
The 446 adversarial questions have no reference answer.
Vendors drop them and score the remaining 1,540.
An audit in April 2026 found 99 wrong labels among those 1,540.
It put the ceiling near 93 under the released answers.
Vendors reporting 92 to 95 are at or above that ceiling, each under its own judge.

slides.caption: A conversation fits inside a modern context window several times over. The scorer's category labels differ from the paper. 446 questions have no answer. 99 labels are wrong.

slides.title: The second benchmark is *better built*
slides.text: Fixed judge, seven types, and two separate columns.

narration: The second benchmark is better designed.
It has a fixed judge model, with over 97 percent agreement with human graders.
It has seven question types, including knowledge updates and abstention.
Its paper keeps retrieval recall and answer accuracy in separate columns.
Its authors measured a frontier model at 0.870 with only the evidence.
With the full history of 115 thousand tokens, the same model scored 0.606.
Vendors now report 90 to 94 with their own readers and judges.
And retrieval-only scores of 96.6 to 100 with no model at all.
The candidate pool averages 48 sessions.
So a retrieval score at k of 50 covers the whole pool and measures nothing.

slides.caption: A fixed judge with 97 percent agreement with humans, seven question types, and separate columns for retrieval and answers. Its authors measured a frontier model at 0.606.

slides.title: The dispute of *2025*

narration: The two largest memory vendors published each other's scores.
In April 2025 one reported the other at 65.99.
In May the other replied.
It had erred in its own earlier claim of 84, and corrected itself to 75.14.
It criticised the first vendor for misconfiguration.
The first vendor's chief technology officer then filed a public issue.
He recomputed the second vendor at 58.44.
Adversarial answers had been counted in a numerator whose denominator excluded them.
Prompts had changed, and one run was compared against ten.
The issue was closed without a reply.
Both vendors now publish scores above 90 on the same benchmark, under newer judges.
None of these numbers is wrong on its own terms.
Together they show the benchmark cannot separate the two systems.

slides.caption: The two largest vendors published each other's scores. One reported 65.99. The other corrected its own 84 to 75.14. The first recomputed that to 58.44. The benchmark cannot separate them.

slides.title: Ten ways a score misleads, *one to five*
items: A k larger than the pool

narration: Here are ten documented ways a published score misleads.
None needs bad faith.
Most are choices a benchmark leaves open.
First, any-hit reported as recall.
On one ranking, 96.6 any-hit at k of five is 91.7 as the TREC fraction.
Second, a k larger than the candidate pool.
At k of 50 over conversations of 19 to 32 sessions, every session is returned.
Recall is 1.0 by construction, and a 100 percent claim was published on exactly that.
Third, a retrieval score placed beside judged answers.
A 96 from one school beside a 72 from the other reads as a 24-point lead that does not exist.
Fourth, the credited target.
A 2026 study moved credit between the raw turn, the session and a canonical form.
Rankings changed on 83 to 94 percent of queries, and the order of systems flipped.
Fifth, category relabelling and denominators.
Three vendors map the same categories three ways.
One dispute turned on answers counted in a numerator whose denominator excluded them.

slides.caption: Any-hit reported as recall. A k larger than the pool. Retrieval beside judged answers. The credited target. Category relabelling and denominators.

slides.title: Ten ways a score misleads, *six to ten*

narration: Sixth, fixes tuned to named questions.
One vendor's file records three fixes written for three failing questions.
It labels them teaching to the test.
Held out, the 100 became 98.4.
Seventh, the vendor as reader and judge.
One vendor scores with the same frontier model as reader and as judge.
Another scores its managed platform with proprietary parts.
There is no standard judge prompt.
Eighth, corrupted or missing gold.
446 questions have no answer.
99 of the remaining 1,540 penalise a correct answer.
Word overlap scores two spellings of the same date as different.
Ninth, single runs.
One vendor published one run against a competitor's ten with standard deviations.
Tenth, synthetic recall as a proxy for reading.
Needle tests do not predict downstream performance.
On the hardest lexical test, eleven of thirteen models lose half their accuracy by 32 thousand tokens.

slides.caption: Fixes tuned to named questions. The vendor as reader and judge. Corrupted or missing gold. Single runs. Synthetic recall as a proxy for reading.

slides.title: Five questions before *believing* a number

narration: Ask five questions before believing a memory number.
Start with the school. Was an answer generated and judged, or was a passage only found?
Second, what unit was retrieved, a session, a turn or a message, and how many candidates were in the pool?
Third, what k, and is k smaller than the pool?
Fourth, who was the reader and who was the judge, and was either the vendor's choice?
Fifth, how many tokens was the corpus, and does that fit inside one call to the reader?
This is the question vendors rarely answer.
A claim that answers all five and still stands is worth a reproduction.
A claim that answers fewer than three is a headline.

slides.caption: Which school? What unit and pool? What k? Whose reader and judge? How many tokens, and does that fit one context window?

slides.title: What to *remember*

narration: Here is what to remember.
Retrieval scores and answer scores are two different quantities, and never share a table.
The two famous benchmarks fit inside one context window, and vendors have saturated them under their own judges.
A score without its unit, its pool and its judge is a headline, not a number.
The benchmarks that reach enterprise scale are far from saturated.
The next page asks whether a long context window makes memory unnecessary.

slides.caption: Two schools, two tables. The two famous benchmarks fit in one context window and are saturated. Ten ways a score misleads. Five questions to ask.
